exercises.prompt:
`x` is `PIC 99 VALUE 10`, and `double-it` doubles its linkage item. The caller runs:

```cobol
    CALL "double-it" USING BY CONTENT x
    DISPLAY x
    CALL "double-it" USING BY REFERENCE x
    DISPLAY x
```

What are the two lines printed? Write them separated by a comma, for example `11, 12`.

feedback.message: Not yet: the first call received a copy, so `x` was still 10 afterwards.
Not yet: `BY CONTENT` doubles a temporary copy and leaves `x` alone.

exercises.solution: The first call doubles a copy, so `x` stays **10**. The second call doubles `x` itself, giving **20**. Output: `10`, then `20`.

exercises.prompt:
A main program runs `CALL "finish-early"` and then `DISPLAY "back in caller"`. The subprogram `finish-early` is:

```cobol
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY "in finish-early"
    STOP RUN.
```

How many lines do these statements print in total?

feedback.message: Not yet: what does `STOP RUN` end, the subprogram or the whole run?

hints: `GOBACK` returns to the caller. `STOP RUN` does something bigger.
exercises.solution: `STOP RUN` ends the entire run unit, caller included, so only `in finish-early` is printed: **1** line. Subprograms should end with `GOBACK`.

exercises.prompt: The subprogram `tick` has `01 calls PIC 99 VALUE 0.` in `WORKING-STORAGE` and `01 fresh PIC 99 VALUE 0.` in `LOCAL-STORAGE`. Each call adds 1 to both and runs `DISPLAY calls " " fresh`. What does the **fourth** call print?

feedback.message: Not yet: local storage is allocated afresh, with its `VALUE`, on every call.
Not yet: working storage keeps its value between calls.

hints: Which section keeps its values from one call to the next?
exercises.solution: Working storage persists, so `calls` reaches 4; local storage starts at its `VALUE` each time, so `fresh` is 1 again. The fourth call prints **`04 01`**.

exercises.prompt: The copybook `EMPREC` contains `05 :TAG:-ID PIC 9(6).` A program says `COPY EMPREC REPLACING ==:TAG:== BY ==NEW-EMP==.` What is the data name of that field in the program?
hints: The pseudo-text `:TAG:` is replaced wherever it appears.
exercises.solution: `:TAG:` becomes `NEW-EMP`, so `:TAG:-ID` becomes **`NEW-EMP-ID`**. Copying the same copybook with different tags gives several copies of one layout with distinct names.

exercises.prompt: A program contains `SELECT employee-file ASSIGN TO EMPMAST`. The job that runs it contains `//EMPMAST DD DSN=PAY.TEST.EMPLOYEE.MASTER,DISP=SHR`. What does `EMPMAST` name?

options.label: A DD name: a label that the job's JCL connects to an actual data set when the program runs.
options.feedback: Yes. Change the `DSN` in the JCL and the same compiled program reads a different data set.

options.label: The name of the data set on disk.
options.feedback: Not yet. The data set is `PAY.TEST.EMPLOYEE.MASTER`; `EMPMAST` is only the label that links it to the program.

options.label: A copybook that describes the record.
options.feedback: Not yet. Copybooks are brought in with `COPY`; `ASSIGN TO` names the external file.

options.label: The name of the COBOL program.
options.feedback: Not yet. The program is named on the `EXEC PGM=` statement.

exercises.solution: `EMPMAST` is a **DD name**. The program refers only to it; the JCL `DD` statement with that name says which data set to use, so tests and production can run the same load module against different files.

exercises.prompt: An embedded `SELECT ... INTO` finds no matching row in Db2. What value does `SQLCODE` hold?

feedback.message: Not yet: 0 means the statement succeeded and returned a row.
Not yet: negative codes are errors; 'no row' is a normal, positive condition.

hints: It is positive and it is a round number.
exercises.solution: **100** means 'row not found' (or, for a cursor, no more rows). 0 is success and negative values are errors, so programs typically `EVALUATE SQLCODE` with those three cases.

exercises.prompt: Why are CICS programs usually written to be pseudo-conversational?

options.label: So that no program holds resources while a person reads and types: the program sends its screen and ends, and CICS starts a new transaction, with the saved state, when the reply arrives.
options.feedback: Yes. That is what lets one CICS region serve thousands of users.

options.label: Because CICS programs cannot read files.
options.feedback: Not yet. They read files and databases all the time, for example with `EXEC CICS READ`.

options.label: Because COBOL has no loops that could wait for input.
options.feedback: Not yet. COBOL has loops; waiting in one would tie up storage and locks for as long as the user takes.

options.label: So that the program can be written without any state.
options.feedback: Not yet. State is still needed; it is handed from one transaction to the next in the COMMAREA or in containers.

hints: Think about how long a person takes to type compared with how long the program takes to run.
exercises.solution: A user may take seconds or minutes to reply, while the program needs milliseconds. In the pseudo-conversational design the program sends its output and ends with `RETURN TRANSID(...) COMMAREA(...)`, freeing everything; CICS starts the next transaction with the saved state when the user responds.
